analysis.one_liner: Taxes pension funds' gains on investments sold within six months, to discourage short-term speculation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced by Senator Kassebaum with Senator Dole in September 1989, it received one Senate Finance Committee hearing in March 1990 and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put an excise tax on gains that large employer pension plans make from selling assets they held for 180 days or less: 10% on assets held 30 days or less, 5% on assets held up to 180 days. Genuine hedging to reduce risk is exempt, and plans with under $1 million in assets are exempt entirely. The goal is to discourage pension funds from constantly trading in and out of investments — 'churning' — and push them toward long-term holdings.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees whose savings sit in large employer pension plans. Churning generates fees and trading costs that are deducted from plan returns, so a tax penalty on quick-turnover gains is meant to steer plan money toward longer-term investments. Long-term investors more generally also benefit if less short-term speculation pressure comes out of the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees in large pension plans

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a 10% excise tax on a large pension plan's gains from selling assets held 30 days or less, and 5% on gains from assets held up to 180 days, directly penalizing rapid in-and-out trading. [S3]
It exempts legitimate hedging transactions identified as risk-reducing, so plans can still protect themselves against price and currency swings without penalty. [S3]
It spares small plans — those with assets under $1 million — from the tax entirely. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large employer pension plans and the institutional investors and Wall Street trading operations that profit from high-volume short-term trading of pension money. The tax is paid out of plan gains, though by design it would change behavior rather than become a large revenue source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large pension funds and Wall Street traders

drawbacks.text: Because pension assets belong to workers, a tax on plan gains is ultimately a charge against retirees' savings; if the tax fails to change trading behavior, it simply reduces plan returns. [S3]
The bill adds recordkeeping and compliance complexity for plan fiduciaries, including look-through rules that tax a plan's share of short-term gains earned inside partnerships it invests in. [S3]

Critics of transaction-style taxes generally argue they can reduce liquidity and market efficiency; the bill's one hearing is the only forum in the record where such objections could have been aired. [S5]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: churning does erode pension returns through fees and trading costs, and a targeted tax on short-turnover gains is a fairly surgical way to discourage it. The main risk is that the tax lands on the plan itself — workers' money — and works only to the extent it actually changes behavior. The design shows care about that problem (hedging is exempt, tiny plans are exempt), but the bill never got far enough for the tradeoffs to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee — one hearing in March 1990, never a markup or floor vote — and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Nancy Kassebaum introduced the bill with Senator Bob Dole on September 21, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. [S5]
The Senate Finance Committee held hearings on the bill on March 21, 1990 (printed as S.Hrg. 101-929), but never reported it out of committee. [S5]
The bill attracted one cosponsor besides its sponsor. [S4]
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutional investors and high-volume pension trading operations, which continue to trade short-term with pension money untaxed. No one gained on the public side from the bill dying.

for.name: Sen. Nancy Landon Kassebaum
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Excessive Churning and Speculation Act of 1989 and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee. [S3][S5]

for.name: Sen. Bob Dole
for.what_they_did: Joined Kassebaum in introducing the bill in the Senate. [S3]

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, held one hearing on March 21, 1990, and never reported it to the full Senate. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Republican-sponsored proposal with one additional Republican cosponsor, but it never reached a vote, so no party split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Institutional investors and Wall Street trading firms
industries.note: A 10% excise tax on gains from assets held 30 days or less directly targets the profits from rapid-turnover trading of pension money. Their loss in this bill is largely the gain of workers' plan returns.

industries.industry: Large employer pension plans and their sponsors
industries.note: Plans with $1 million or more in assets would owe the tax on short-term gains, but those assets are workers' retirement savings, so the bill is designed to change plan behavior rather than simply take money out.
